instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only

# Continual-ARC reasoning

Use this skill for ARC-style tasks in a recurring puzzle stream, especially when the interaction allows requesting demonstrations and submission attempts are costly.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the interaction contract.** Preserve the required response format exactly; choose one action per turn. Treat demo requests and wrong submissions as costly, and do not spend either without a reason.
2. **Inspect demonstrations comparatively.** Track dimensions, background, marker/object colors, and every changed cell. Form a compact rule that explains all examples, rather than fitting only the most visually salient region.
3. **Separate evidence from hypothesis.** Prefer a rule that predicts multiple independent changes in each demo. If ambiguity remains and the cost is justified, request another demo before submitting.
4. **Apply the rule mechanically.** Use a small script or structured representation for large grids when useful. Preserve original marker cells and untouched background; do not rely on manual transcription for a long output.
5. **Validate before submitting.** Check row count, column count, allowed values, unchanged source cells where appropriate, and consistency of every changed cell with the inferred transformation. Re-read the exact test input when constructing the result.
6. **Submit only the requested artifact.** In strict ARC interaction formats, avoid explanatory text if the protocol calls for a single action object.

## Common geometric transformation: connect aligned markers

A recurring pattern is a sparse set of same-color marker cells on a uniform background. Demonstrations may show a third color filling the straight gaps between consecutive markers that share a row or column. See [references/aligned-marker-lines.md](references/aligned-marker-lines.md) for how to infer and implement this rule, including boundary and overlap checks.

### Validated recurrence: task-83eba677 horizontal gap fill

For task-83eba677, fill only the cells strictly between consecutive same-color markers in each row with color 2. Do not fill vertical alignments, even when markers share a column. Preserve marker cells and all unrelated background cells. This holds for single-cell gaps as well as longer gaps: a newly accepted 18×24 test (background 4, markers 8) had horizontal marker runs spanning gaps of several cells; every intervening cell between consecutive 8s in a row became 2, with other cells unchanged. Prior fresh cases also confirmed background 6/marker 1 and background 3/marker 5, plus an accepted 17×13 background 1/marker 8 case (29 changed cells). The 5×6 case had pairs at row 2 columns 0/2 and row 4 columns 1/3 (0-based), yielding 2 at the intervening cells only. Infer fill color 2, not from background or marker color.

## Full-line recoloring (validated task-5ebf4030)

For task-5ebf4030, identify complete horizontal rows and vertical columns consisting entirely of the same non-background color (color 7 in the demo; color 3 and 6 in fresh tests). Recolor every cell of each such full line to 2. Preserve all other cells, including occurrences of the line color outside complete lines. A newly solved 6×27 test had background 1 and line color 6; the only full row was row 2 (0-based), and full columns were 11, 19, and 25. Recolor those four lines to 2 while retaining partial 6s elsewhere. The demo had a full vertical line and a full horizontal line; the fresh 28x9 test had two full vertical lines and two full horizontal lines. This criterion reproduced the demo output and was accepted on fresh tests with two full vertical and two full horizontal lines (28x9), and on a 20x10 test with complete horizontal rows 3, 4, 5, 8, 10 and complete vertical column 4 (0-based). The latter confirms that full lines are recognized by the uniform line color even when the surrounding grid is a mixed 8/6 field; all complete 6-lines become 2. A second fresh 21x25 test used color 5, with complete rows 4 and 13 (0-based) and complete columns 10, 12, 17, and 22; all these lines became 2 while all other cells were preserved. Apply only to full single-color lines, not merely dense or partial alignments.

## Validated motif-stamping substrate

For task-868ab99b, extract the foreground mask of the uniquely colored seed motif and stamp that mask in its seed color at every translation where **all occupied mask offsets overlay 0-cells**. The dominant field color can vary (e.g. 8 or 9) and is not the placement substrate; requiring mask offsets to match the dominant color is wrong. Ignore mask bounding-box cells that are not foreground, and preserve all cells outside the stamped mask. This rule reproduced the provided demos and a fresh test.

For task-7a5e2600, the compact color-5 seed motif is the 6-cell mask with offsets (from its top-left): (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), and (3,2). Stamp this mask in color 5 at every translation where all occupied offsets overlay cells of color 0; replace only those zero cells and preserve all other cells, including the seed and nonzero field. A fresh 22×17 test (background 6) was accepted with this exact rule. Do not require the entire bounding box to be zero: only the six motif offsets determine valid placement.

Do not infer motif substrate rules universally; for other tasks, determine the mask, seed color, and placement substrate from demonstrations.

### Validated recurrence: task-7a5e2600 motif stamping

The compact color-5 seed motif is the 6-cell mask with offsets (from its top-left): (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), and (3,2). Stamp this mask in color 5 at every translation where all occupied offsets overlay cells of color 0; replace only those zero cells and preserve all other cells, including the seed and nonzero field. A fresh 22×17 test (background 6) was accepted with this exact rule. Do not require the entire bounding box to be zero: only the six motif offsets determine valid placement.

## Periodic stripe completion (validated task-eca8fe17)

For task-eca8fe17, demos show a sparse periodic color field encoded by colored full stripes/lines. Infer the repeating cycle and orientation from the line markers, then tile that cycle across the whole grid, replacing zeros as well as preserving the encoded colors. Examples: horizontal stripes can encode a row-period cycle (period 6 in the 8x8 demo; period 7 in the 11x11 demo), while parallel slope-−1 diagonal stripes encode phases of a cycle by `row+column mod period` (period 4 in the 28x28 demo). For fresh tests, do not assume one orientation or period; identify line direction and phase-color mapping from the current input/demos. Validated mappings include: a 28×28 parallel slope−1 diagonal field with period 4 encoded by `(r+c) mod 4`, phases 0→4, 1→2, 2→1; and task-eca8fe17 fresh tests where `(r+c) mod 3` mapped phases 0→4, 1→2, 2→1. A separate 8×8 test had parallel slope+1 diagonal markers, period 5 encoded by `(r−c) mod 5`, with phases 0→1, 1→9, 2→6, 3→5, 4→3; fill every cell using this cycle while preserving the encoded marker colors. A successful 23×23 test had a period-3 slope+1 diagonal field, with `c−r mod 3 = 0,1,2` mapped to colors `6,6,2` respectively (equivalently, color 2 at `c−r ≡ 2 mod 3`, color 6 elsewhere); marker 2s fixed that phase and overlapping 6 diagonal bands confirmed the remaining phase assignments. Fill every cell with the periodic field, not merely extending gaps.

### Confirmed task-eca8fe17 horizontal full-row cycle fresh test
A 7×7 test had each row uniform, with row colors `[0,9,3,6,9,8,0]`. Correct output row colors were `[8,9,3,6,9,8,9]`, i.e. repeat the six-row cycle `[8,9,3,6,9,8]` from row 0. The colored rows at indices 1–5 validated this period and phase; zeros at rows 0 and 6 were unknown slots, not cycle colors. Accepted. Infer the smallest supported periodic sequence and fill zero rows; preserve the demonstrated cycle colors.

## Noisy rectangular-field reconstruction (validated task-7a9d058a)

The grid is a patchwork of uniform rectangular color regions on a uniform background, corrupted by sparse arbitrary noise symbols. Recover the region layout from repeated full spans and intact portions; recolor every cell (including distractors on the background and outliers inside a region) to its underlying region color. Do not preserve apparent outliers merely because they lie outside a foreground rectangle; do not treat one digit as a globally bad color or assume zero means empty. In the demonstrated 13×17 case, the background was 1, with a 4×4 region of 2, separate 4-colored rectangles, and a 2×6 block of 8; scattered values such as 0, 3, 5, and 9 were corruption, so background intrusions reverted to 1 and within-region defects reverted to the region color. In the 25×26 test, the true background was 9 and rectangular fields were 8 and 4. The accepted output confirms that isolated non-9 marks outside the coherent rectangles (including isolated marks adjacent to or apparently aligned with them) revert to 9, while anomalies inside rectangles restore to 8/4. Determine exact bounds by row/column continuity and inspect all boundary rows/columns; do not extend a rectangle from a singleton or merely nearby/aligned speckle. The first submission was rejected; the successful correction required careful rect bounds and clearing all exterior noise, not retaining it as foreground. Validate the entire predicted grid against this field layout before submitting.

## Comparing aligned panels with sparse zero-cells

When a divider separates aligned panels, infer the cellwise predicate from the demos rather than assuming that each panel's modal color defines its semantic background. In the validated task-192705d2 pattern, output a 2 where both corresponding input cells are nonzero, and 0 otherwise. The panels can have different dominant colors (for example, 5 on one side and 0 on the other; or 8 and 6 on a fresh test), while literal 0 is the empty-cell value. Thus implement `left_cell != 0 and right_cell != 0`; do not implement “both are non-background relative to each panel’s mode,” which incorrectly selects shared zeros in a 8/6 test. This was confirmed by a rejected shared-zero candidate followed by a correct nonzero-overlap submission. A fresh 4×9 recurrence had a single divider column (color 1) between two 4×4 panels; exclude the divider and produce a 4×4 mask by the same nonzero-overlap predicate. A further accepted 7×27 test used a full horizontal divider row (color 6) between 3×27 panels (dominant colors 1 and 9); exclude the divider and output the 3×27 nonzero-overlap mask. This confirms the same predicate applies to horizontal as well as vertical panel splits. Always replay the predicate against the demo outputs and exact fresh input before submitting.

## Validated task-65d930f4 three-band mirror tiling

For task-65d930f4, expand an H×W input to 3H×2W. Each output row is the input row mirrored left-to-right, concatenated with the original row. Stack three vertical bands: input rows bottom-to-top, then top-to-bottom, then bottom-to-top. Equivalently, output row source indices are `H-1..0`, `0..H-1`, `H-1..0`. Preserve all source cell values; this is a geometric reflection/tiling rule, not recoloring. Confirmed on the 5×4 demo (15×8 output), a fresh 3×9 test (9×18 output), and a fresh 1×12 test (3×24 output). For the 1×12 input `[5,0,1,3,4,3,7,6,9,3,2,8]`, each of the three output rows was `[8,2,3,9,6,7,3,4,3,1,0,5,5,0,1,3,4,3,7,6,9,3,2,8]`; accepted.

## Pitfalls

- A marker may belong to both a horizontal and a vertical segment; preserve the marker color at intersections.
- Fill only the gap between consecutive markers in a row or column unless demos establish extrapolation or another endpoint rule.
- A visually plausible line rule is still a hypothesis until all demo changes are explained. In particular, inspect apparent extra fills as possible perpendicular segments before concluding they are unexplained.
- Keep coordinates and row/column indexing explicit to avoid one-cell shifts.
